primary_meaning: In Christian interpretation the term 'week' (Hebrew shabua, literally 'a seven' or 'heptad') is most commonly treated symbolically as a unit of seven years rather than seven days, especially in Daniel's prophecy of the seventy weeks, where nearly all traditions—dispensationalist, historicist, and most critical scholars alike—read each 'week' as seven years (seventy weeks = 490 years). More broadly, the week functions as a symbol of divine order and completeness rooted in the seven-day creation pattern, culminating in the Sabbath rest.
primary_basis: Daniel 9:24-27 (the seventy weeks determined upon Daniel's people)
Genesis 29:27-28 ('fulfill her week' = seven years of service for Rachel)
Leviticus 25:8 (seven sabbaths of years, forty-nine years, as background for the week-of-years concept)
Genesis 1:1-2:3 and Exodus 20:8-11 (the creation week establishing the seven-day pattern and Sabbath)
Numbers 14:34 and Ezekiel 4:6 (the day-for-a-year principle often invoked to justify reading weeks as years)

alternatives.meaning: The 'week' of Daniel 9 read as seven literal years with the seventieth week deferred to a future seven-year tribulation period (the dispensationalist 'gap' reading); the week is still seven years, but its placement and eschatological function differ materially from continuous-fulfillment readings.
basis: Revelation 11:2-3; 12:6, 14; 13:5 (the 1260 days / 42 months / time, times, and half a time correlated with half of Daniel's final week)

alternatives.meaning: The seventy weeks as a symbolic, non-arithmetical figure of completeness (ten jubilees or simply 'fullness of time') rather than an exact 490-year chronology; found among some critical scholars, amillennial interpreters, and idealist readings.
basis: Matthew 18:22 (seventy times seven as symbolic totality)

alternatives.meaning: The 'cosmic week' or sex-/septa-millennial scheme: the seven days of creation as a template for world history, with each day representing a thousand years and the seventh 'day' the millennial Sabbath rest; prominent among some church fathers (Epistle of Barnabas, Irenaeus, Lactantius, Augustine early on) and revived by some modern premillennialists.

The week as a liturgical/typological symbol of the Christian life and new creation, with the eighth day (Sunday, resurrection day) transcending the old week; common in patristic and liturgical theology rather than prophetic interpretation.
basis: John 20:1, 19, 26 (appearances on the first day / eighth day)

alternatives.meaning: Weeks in Daniel taken as literal seven-day weeks (490 days); occasionally proposed but rejected by virtually all traditions.
basis: Daniel 10:2-3 ('three full weeks' of literal days, used to argue Daniel could distinguish literal weeks)

notes: There is strong cross-traditional agreement that 'week' in prophetic contexts (Daniel 9) symbolizes a heptad of years, and that the week generally carries the symbolism of the number seven—completeness, divine order, and the creation-Sabbath rhythm. The genuine disputes are downstream: how the seventy weeks are computed, whether the seventieth week is past or future, and whether the figure is exact chronology or symbolic totality. 'Week' by itself is less frequently treated as a standalone symbol than 'seven' or 'Sabbath,' so the consensus centers on the week-of-years usage in Daniel and the creation-week pattern.
